choices: Add `if (isActivityFinishingOrDestroyed()) return;` before showing the dialog
Wrap `showDefaultBrowserDialog()` in a try/catch for `WindowManager.BadTokenException`
Post the dialog with `PostTask.postTask()` so it runs on the UI thread
Nothing — dialogs are safe to show from any callback once `onCreate()` has run
explain: Activities can be destroyed between when a callback is scheduled and when it runs. Guard UI work in async callbacks, animation listeners, and lambdas with `isActivityFinishingOrDestroyed()`.

choices: `if (getView() == null) return;` is sufficient, since a detached fragment has no view
`if (!isAdded() || isDetached()) return;`, then bail if `getActivity()` is null/finishing
`if (result == null) return;` — fragment state doesn't matter for Mojo responses on the UI thread
Check `isResumed()` and queue the update until `onResume()` otherwise
explain: Fragments can be detached or their Activity destroyed while async work runs. Verify `isAdded()`/`!isDetached()` and that the host Activity is non-null and not finishing before touching UI.

choices: Debounce clicks with a 500 ms timer stored in a static field on the fragment
Return `false` from the listener so the preference ignores subsequent clicks until done
Call `preference.setEnabled(false)` before the request; re-enable it in the callback
Show a toast telling the user the email is being sent
explain: Disable interactive UI while an async operation is in flight to prevent double-clicks, then re-enable it when the callback completes.

choices: The null check in `showSplash()` is redundant and should be removed for consistency with `hideSplash()`
`mSplashContainer` should be made `static` so it is never null
Nothing — `View.GONE` on a null view is a no-op
Add the same null check to `hideSplash()`; the field is treated as nullable elsewhere
explain: If a member field is null-checked in some code paths, check it in all paths that use it. Inconsistent checks suggest some paths can crash.

choices: Add an explicit `if (!view_counter_service_) return;`; it may be null in incognito
Leave it; upstream guarantees the call never happens in incognito
Replace it with `CHECK(view_counter_service_)` so a null service in incognito crashes loudly
Create the service on demand for the incognito profile inside the bridge
explain: Services reached through bridges or native code may be null for incognito profiles. Add explicit null checks at the point of use, even if upstream theoretically handles it.

prompt: You need a thread-safe singleton for `BraveAccountServiceFactory`. Which implementation follows the standard?
choices: A `static final Object sLock` with a `synchronized (sLock)` null-check in `getInstance()`
A private static `LazyHolder` nested class with a `static final INSTANCE` field
A `volatile` static field with double-checked locking
Initialize the instance in `Application.onCreate()` and expose it via a public static field
explain: Use the LazyHolder idiom for singleton factories instead of explicit `synchronized` lock blocks. It's compact and thread-safe thanks to Java's class-loading guarantees.

prompt: A custom `Preference` stores `mTextColor = resolveThemeColor(context, R.attr.textColor)` in its constructor. Users report the title stays dark after switching to dark theme. What's the fix?
choices: Cache the color in a static field shared by all instances of the preference
Hardcode the color with `Color.parseColor()` in the constructor
Resolve the theme color in `onBindViewHolder()` and apply it there
Recreate the whole settings Activity whenever the theme changes
explain: Resolve theme colors at bind time (`onBindViewHolder` or equivalent), not during construction, so they update correctly on light/dark switches without recreating the view.

prompt: A preference in `brave_main_preferences.xml` is removed in Java when a feature flag is off. QA notices it briefly flashes on screen before disappearing. What should you add to the XML?
choices: `android:enabled="false"` on the preference
`android:visibility="gone"` on the preference's layout
`app:singleLineTitle="false"` on the preference
`app:isPreferenceVisible="false"` on the preference
explain: For preferences that are hidden or removed programmatically based on a flag, set `app:isPreferenceVisible="false"` in XML to avoid the brief visual flash.

choices: Add an `assert` with the same condition above the guard, keeping the fallback
Replace the guard with `throw new IllegalArgumentException()` to fail fast on bad input
Upgrade `Log.e` to `Log.wtf` and remove the early return
Remove the guard; invalid addresses should be impossible here
explain: Pair log-only defensive checks with `assert`: asserts surface problems immediately in debug builds, while the graceful handling still protects release builds.

prompt: `hasPipPermission()` queries `PackageManager` and `AppOpsManager`, and it's being called from a frequently-hit path. A teammate suggests caching it in a member during `onCreate()`. What's the right consideration?
choices: Always cache system service results; they never change during an Activity's lifetime
Cache expensive lookups, but not values that can change unnotified, like PiP availability
Never cache system service results; Android already caches `PackageManager` lookups internally
Move the lookup to a background thread instead of caching it
explain: Compute expensive system-service lookups once and store them instead of repeating them in a hot path. The exception is values that can change without notification in multi-window or config-change scenarios, such as PiP availability.

prompt: You're adding wallet address validation to an Android screen. iOS and desktop accept the same input. What should you do first?
choices: Write a Java regex validator, since Android needs to validate before calling native
Copy the iOS Swift validation logic into Kotlin for parity
Check whether unified validation already exists on the core/native side and use it
Skip validation on Android and rely on server errors
explain: Before writing validation in Android/Java, check for unified core/native-side validation. Preferring core-side logic avoids inconsistencies across Android, iOS, and desktop.

prompt: A Robolectric test crashes because the code under test calls `ChromeFeatureList.isEnabled(BraveFeatureList.SOME_FEATURE)`. What's the recommended pattern in the production code?
choices: Wrap the call in `try { ... } catch (UnsatisfiedLinkError e) {}`
Convert the test to an instrumentation test; Robolectric can't test this code
Load the native library in the test with `System.loadLibrary()`
Guard the call with `if (FeatureList.isNativeInitialized())`
explain: Robolectric has no native/JNI. Use conditional checks like `FeatureList.isNativeInitialized()` to handle the test environment gracefully (see `BraveDynamicColors.java`).

prompt: Your bytecode class adapter for an upstream Java class keeps failing. The class has two constructors. What's the accepted approach?
choices: Use a direct `.java.patch` file for that class instead
Add a third constructor so the adapter can choose a unique one
Copy the whole upstream class into `brave/` and redirect all imports
Disable the adapter and use reflection to change the behavior at runtime
explain: Bytecode (class adapter) patching fails when a class has two constructors; use a direct `.java.patch` instead. Likewise, use direct `BUILD.gn` patches when circular deps prevent using `java_sources.gni`.

prompt: Presubmit flags `ProfileManager.getLastUsedRegularProfile()` in `QuickActionSearchAndBookmarkWidgetProvider`. As the reviewer, what do you say?
choices: Block the PR until the profile comes from the hosting Activity's `getProfile()` instead
Accept it: widget providers have no Activity or WebContents context, like upstream widgets
Replace it with `ProfileManager.getOriginalProfile()`, which presubmit allows in widget code
Pass the profile into the widget through an Intent extra
explain: Never flag `getLastUsedRegularProfile()` as a violation in Android widget providers, where no Activity/WebContents context exists. Upstream Chromium does the same in its widgets.

choices: Keep it but mark it `@Deprecated` so nobody starts depending on it yet
Keep it and add a TODO linking to the future issue that will use it
Remove it before merging; unused interfaces shouldn't be left in the codebase
Make it package-private so it can't leak into the public API until someone needs it
explain: Don't leave unused interfaces, listener patterns, or helper methods behind. If they were scaffolded during development and never used, remove them before merging.

prompt:
```xml
<FrameLayout
    android:id="@+id/splash_animation_container"
    android:clickable="true"
    android:focusable="true"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content" />
```
The container only hosts a display-only Lottie animation. What should the reviewer say?
choices: Also add `android:contentDescription` so TalkBack can announce the animation
Keep `focusable` but remove `clickable`, so keyboard users can reach it
Fine as-is — it stops touches from passing through to the views below the splash
Drop `clickable`/`focusable`; they hurt accessibility and touch handling here
explain: Don't set `android:clickable` or `android:focusable` on purely decorative or display-only views like animation containers; these attributes change accessibility and touch event handling.

prompt: Android and iOS both ship the exact same onboarding Lottie JSON file, each in its own directory. A designer updates the animation. What does the standard recommend?
choices: Keep a single shared copy that both platforms reference
Keep per-platform copies so each team can evolve them independently
Generate the Android copy from the iOS one with a build step
Convert the Android copy to an `AnimatedVectorDrawable`
explain: When Android and iOS use identical assets, reference a single shared copy instead of maintaining duplicates, so changes only need to be made once.

prompt: `brave_java_sources.gni` now lists dozens of `crypto_wallet` Java files mixed with everything else. What's the suggested improvement?
choices: Sort the list alphabetically so the wallet files are grouped
Consider moving the feature's sources into a separate build target
Split `brave_java_sources.gni` into two `.gni` files of roughly equal size
Nothing — all Brave Java sources should live in one list
explain: When feature-specific Java sources accumulate in `brave_java_sources.gni`, consider a separate build target for better build isolation and dependency tracking.

prompt: Which version of `handleState()` follows the Brave Android style?
choices: `if (!isFinished) { if (hasData) { /* main logic */ } }`
`if (!isFinished && hasData) { /* main logic */ } else { return; }`
`if (isFinished) return;` and `if (!hasData) return;`, then the main logic
Move the main logic to a helper and call it from inside both nested `if` blocks
explain: When a condition decides whether the rest of a method runs, return early instead of nesting `if` blocks; it reduces nesting depth and improves readability.

prompt: A PR modifies a class adapter in `build/android/bytecode/java/org/brave/bytecode/`. What else should it include?
choices: A Robolectric unit test that instantiates the patched class and calls its methods
A note in the PR description; bytecode adapters are verified at build time
A ProGuard keep rule for every method the adapter touches
`BytecodeTest.java` entries in `testClassesExist` and `testMethodsExist`
explain: Bytecode adapter changes need a matching bytecode test in `BytecodeTest.java` (class existence and method existence with return types), so upstream refactors fail at test time, not silently at runtime.

prompt: A new instrumentation test needs a class kept from shrinking. The author adds the `-keep` rule to `android/java/proguard.flags`. What's the right feedback?
choices: Move it to `apk_for_test.flags`; `proguard.flags` is for runtime reflection only
Correct — all keep rules belong in `proguard.flags`, test or production
Add it to both `.flags` files to be safe, since test APKs merge them anyway
Use `@Keep` on the class instead, which R8 only honors in test builds
explain: Keep rules for runtime reflection go in `proguard.flags`. Test-only rules go in `apk_for_test.flags`; putting them in `proguard.flags` grows the production APK by preventing shrinking.

choices: `List.of` is immutable, so `register()` will throw on insert; use `new ArrayList<>()`
The constructor may run before `sEntries` is set; register in a `static {}` block after it
`sEntries` should be `volatile` so other threads see it initialized
There's no risk; Java always initializes a subclass's statics before its constructor runs
explain: A redirected allocation inside `UpstreamClass` static init can re-enter `BraveClass()` before `BraveClass`'s statics are initialized. Keep redirected constructors free of reads of their own static state; use a static block placed after the fields it uses.

prompt: You change a private method to package-private only so a test in the same package can call it. Which annotation should you add?
choices: `@VisibleForTesting` with no arguments, since package-private is already the default
`@SuppressWarnings("unused")`
`@VisibleForTesting(otherwise = VisibleForTesting.PRIVATE)`
No annotation; a `// for testing` comment is enough
explain: Annotate members made package-private solely for tests with `@VisibleForTesting(otherwise = VisibleForTesting.PRIVATE)`. It documents intent and lets IDEs flag misuse from non-test code.

prompt: You need to add one Brave button to an upstream toolbar. A teammate proposes copying the whole upstream layout XML into Brave and adding the button there. Best response?
choices: Good idea — XML replacement is the cleanest, most readable way to customize upstream UI
Patch the upstream XML file in place with a `.patch` instead, which keeps the diff minimal
Use reflection to inject the button into the toolbar after layout inflation
Add it programmatically via `addView`; replace the XML only if that's equally invasive
explain: Replacing full upstream XML layouts creates maintenance burden during Chromium upgrades. Prefer programmatic `addView`, unless that requires extending final classes or is equally invasive; then document the trade-off.

prompt: You're adding a brand-new Brave-only drawable, `ic_brave_vpn_badge.xml`. Where should it go?
choices: In a dedicated `brave-res` folder
In the upstream `chrome/android/java/res/drawable/` directory next to similar icons
In whichever upstream folder the consuming layout lives in
In `res/raw/` so it isn't merged with upstream resources
explain: Brave-specific resources go in `brave-res`. Upstream resource directories are only for intentionally overriding an existing upstream resource; otherwise it's unclear whether a file is an addition or an override.

prompt: A PR removes an Android feature by deleting its Java classes and its settings XML. What should the reviewer check before approving?
choices: That the deleted classes were marked `@Deprecated` for one release before removal
That related bytecode adapters/tests, ProGuard rules, JNI, flags, and GN refs are removed
Only that the build still compiles; any leftover references are harmless since R8 prunes them
That the strings are kept in the `.grd` in case the feature returns later
explain: When removing a feature, audit all artifacts: bytecode adapters, ProGuard rules, bytecode test entries, Java sources, resources, JNI bindings, feature flags, and build references.

choices: Keep it for safety in case the min SDK is ever lowered again
Add an `else` branch that logs a warning for unsupported devices
Remove the check; it's dead code given the min SDK
Replace it with `BuildInfo.isAtLeastM()` for readability
explain: Remove Android version checks for API levels below the app's minimum SDK (e.g. Lollipop/Marshmallow); they're dead code.

prompt: You're writing a direct (non-`chromium_src`) patch to an upstream Java file. Which approach minimizes conflicts on Chromium upgrades?
choices: Edit the existing upstream line in place so the diff stays as small as possible
Reformat the surrounding block so the patch has clear anchors
Comment out the upstream line and add your version below it
Add entirely new lines rather than editing existing upstream lines
explain: In direct patches, prefer adding new lines over modifying existing ones. New lines have no upstream anchor that might change, reducing conflicts during upgrades.

prompt: You need to change behavior inside an anonymous inner class in upstream Chromium Java code, and the Brave override system can't handle it. What's acceptable?
choices: Use a `.patch`, explain why in the PR, and link the override-support tracking issue
Rewrite the whole upstream class as a Brave subclass and redirect it via bytecode
Use reflection at runtime to swap out the anonymous class instance after construction
Drop the change; anonymous inner classes can't be customized
explain: When the override system can't handle anonymous inner classes, a `.patch` file is the accepted fallback; document the reason and link to the tracking issue.

prompt: A PR tweaks a color in `brave_colors.xml` to fix the contrast on one new screen. What should the reviewer ask?
choices: Why not hardcode the color in that one layout instead?
Were other UIs using this resource checked for impact?
Can the color be moved into upstream's `colors.xml` instead?
Nothing — color tweaks are low risk
explain: Shared resource values (colors, dimensions, styles) can affect many screens. Cross-check every usage before modifying them.

prompt: A button looks wrong in dark mode. Which fix aligns with the standard?
choices: Patch the upstream Java class to call `setTextColor()` based on the current night-mode flag
Override `onConfigurationChanged()` and recolor the button manually
Use baseline XML color resources for non-dynamic states; test with Dynamic Colors on/off
Disable Dynamic Colors for this screen so the color is predictable
explain: For theming issues, follow upstream: baseline colors (XML resources) for non-dynamic states rather than patching Java to set colors. Always verify with the Dynamic Colors flag enabled and disabled.

prompt: You need a new Android string for a Brave feature. Where should it go?
choices: In upstream `chrome_strings.grd`, next to related strings
In the upstream `strings.xml` of the module that uses it, for locality
Hardcoded in Java until translations are ready
In `android_brave_strings.grd` or another Brave-owned resource
explain: Never modify upstream string resource files like `chrome_strings.grd`. Brave strings go in `android_brave_strings.grd` or a Brave-owned file to avoid patch conflicts.

choices: Add `@NullUnmarked` to the override to match upstream
Add `@NonNull` to `profile` to be stricter than upstream
Add `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")` instead; it's equivalent
Nothing — overrides inherit annotations automatically
explain: Match upstream nullability annotations (`@NullUnmarked`, `@Nullable`, `@NonNull`) on overrides. Mismatches cause NullAway build failures.

prompt: Which Log TAG declaration in `BraveVpnProfileController` follows the guideline?
choices: `private static final String TAG = "BraveVpnProfileController";`
`private static final String TAG = "BraveVPN";`
`private static final String TAG = BraveVpnProfileController.class.getSimpleName();`
`private static final String TAG = "org.chromium.chrome.browser.vpn.BraveVpnProfileController";`
explain: Log TAGs should be short and descriptive, not a repeat of the full class name when that adds no value.

prompt: Which XML follows the Brave Android layout guideline?
choices: `<View android:paddingStart="16dp" android:paddingEnd="16dp" />`
`<View android:paddingLeft="16dp" android:paddingRight="16dp" />`
`<View android:paddingHorizontal="16dp" />`
`<View android:padding="16dp" android:paddingTop="0dp" android:paddingBottom="0dp" />`
explain: Use shorthand attributes (`paddingHorizontal`, `marginHorizontal`, `paddingVertical`, `marginVertical`) instead of setting start/end or top/bottom separately.

prompt: With NullAway in JSpecify mode, which field declaration is correct?
choices: `@Nullable` on its own line, then `private String mValue;` on the next
`@Nullable private String mValue;`
`private String @Nullable mValue;`
`private @Nullable String mValue;`
explain: In JSpecify mode `@Nullable` is `TYPE_USE`, so it must go immediately before the type (e.g. `private @Nullable String`, or `Outer.@Nullable Inner`).

prompt: With JSpecify-style `@Nullable`, which declaration is a **non-null list of nullable strings**?
choices: `List<@Nullable String> mList;`
`@Nullable List<String> mList;`
`List<String> @Nullable mList;`
`@Nullable List<@Nullable String> mList;`
explain: Position matters: the annotation applies to the type it precedes. `List<@Nullable String>` is a non-null list whose elements may be null.

choices: Annotate the method with `@Initializer`
Annotate the method with `@RequiresNonNull("mNullableString")`
Change the field to non-null and suppress the constructor warning
Copy the field to a local `boolean isSet` and check that
explain: NullAway analyzes per method, so use `@RequiresNonNull`, `@EnsuresNonNull`, `@EnsuresNonNullIf`, and `@Contract` to carry nullness conditions across method boundaries. `@RequiresNonNull` only makes sense on private methods.

prompt: A field is null until `doThing()` first sets it, and is never set back to null. NullAway warns when it's used later inside a `PostTask` lambda. Which annotation fits best?
choices: `@Nullable`, plus `assumeNonNull()` inside every lambda
`@NullUnmarked` on the class
`@MonotonicNonNull`
`@Initializer` on `doThing()`
explain: For fields that start null but are never reset to null after initialization, use `@MonotonicNonNull`. NullAway then trusts the field stays non-null after assignment, even in lambdas.

prompt: `obj.getNullableString()` returns null only in a broken state, and a null would cause worse problems later if it slipped through. You want a crash even in production. Which do you use?
choices: `assumeNonNull(ret)`
`assert ret != null : "broken";`
`assertNonNull(ret)`
`Objects.requireNonNull(ret)`
explain: `Objects.requireNonNull()` crashes in production; use it when null would cause worse problems later. `assumeNonNull`, `assertNonNull`, and `assert` don't crash in prod (asserts only fire on Canary as dump-without-crashing).

prompt: You need a non-null **expression** to assign a field from a map lookup, with assert semantics. Which is idiomatic?
choices: `mNonNullField = assertNonNull(dict.get("key"));` with `import static`
`mNonNullField = NullUtil.assertNonNull(dict.get("key"));` without a static import
`assert dict.get("key") != null; mNonNullField = dict.get("key");`
`mNonNullField = (String) dict.get("key");`
explain: Use `assertNonNull()` when you need an assert as an expression, and always use `import static` for `assumeNonNull`/`assertNonNull`.

prompt: A class has a `destroy()` method that nulls out `mService`, which is otherwise always non-null. NullAway complains. What does the guide recommend?
choices: Mark the whole class `@NullUnmarked`, since lifecycle nulling is outside NullAway's model
Make it `@Nullable` with an `@EnsuresNonNullIf` guard, or suppress NullAway on `destroy()`
Never null fields in `destroy()`; leave the references alive until GC collects the object
Annotate `destroy()` with `@Initializer` so NullAway treats the field as reassigned there
explain: For destroy-nulled fields, choose one of two strategies: `@Nullable` fields guarded by an `@EnsuresNonNullIf` check (preferred for complex cases), or suppress warnings on `destroy()` (simpler cases).

choices: Yes — NullAway can't see through method calls, so an inline `mService != null` check is required
Yes — `@EnsuresNonNullIf` only works when `result = true`
No — `result = false` means `mService` is non-null whenever `isDestroyed()` is false
No, but only because `doWork()` is public and NullAway skips public entry points
explain: Destruction strategy 1 (preferred for complex cases): keep the field `@Nullable` and guard uses with an `@EnsuresNonNullIf(..., result = false)` `isDestroyed()` helper, which NullAway trusts.

prompt: A simple class keeps `mService` non-null for its whole life except that `destroy()` sets it to null. What's the simple, recommended approach?
choices: Mark `destroy()` `@NullUnmarked` so callers also skip null checks
Make the field `@Nullable` and add `assumeNonNull(mService)` at every use
Make the field `@MonotonicNonNull` so it may be set to null once
Keep it non-null; add `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")` to `destroy()`
explain: Destruction strategy 2 (simpler cases): leave the field non-null and suppress NullAway warnings on `destroy()` only.

prompt: A RecyclerView binder sets `mField1`/`mField2` in `onBindViewHolder()`. To silence NullAway, the author adds `@Initializer` to `onBindViewHolder()`. What's the right feedback?
choices: Don't; use an `@EnsuresNonNull` `assertBound()` helper, as binding isn't construction
Good — `@Initializer` is exactly for binder methods that set fields before first use
Use `@NullUnmarked` on the binder class instead, since RecyclerView controls binding
Initialize both fields to empty placeholder views in the constructor so they're never null
explain: `onBindViewHolder()` isn't a real initializer. Add an `assertBound()` helper annotated `@EnsuresNonNull({...})` that asserts the fields, and call it in methods that need them.

choices: Annotate the class `@NullUnmarked`, since it's just a plain data struct with no logic to check
Make the fields `final`, set them in a constructor, and use `/* title= */` at call sites
Initialize both fields to `""` at declaration so they're never null for readers
Add `@MonotonicNonNull` to each field so they can be assigned after construction
explain: NullAway warns on non-primitive, non-`@Nullable` public fields not set by a constructor. Add a constructor that sets all fields, with `/* paramName= */` comments for readability.

prompt: `getTabById()` is `@Nullable`, but many callers know the tab exists and dislike the null checks. A teammate proposes changing its return type to non-null. Best response?
choices: Agree — annotate it `@NonNull` since callers expect non-null
Have callers wrap each call in `Objects.requireNonNull()`
Keep it `@Nullable`; add `getTabByIdChecked()` returning `assertNonNull(getTabById(id))`
Annotate the method `@NullUnmarked` so callers that know the tab exists stop getting warnings
explain: Don't mis-annotate `@Nullable` methods as non-null; it hides real nullability. For Chromium-authored code, add a "Checked" companion for callers that know the value exists.

prompt: You need to pass a `Supplier<@Nullable String>` to a method taking `Supplier<String>`, and you know it never returns null here. What's the idiomatic call?
choices: `acceptsNonNullSupplier(nullableSupplier);` — the compiler handles variance
`acceptsNonNullSupplier(() -> nullableSupplier.get());`
Annotate the parameter `@NullUnmarked`
`acceptsNonNullSupplier(SupplierUtils.asNonNull(nullableSupplier));`
explain: `Supplier<T>` and `Supplier<@Nullable T>` aren't assignment-compatible due to generics invariance. Use `SupplierUtils.asNonNull()` (or an explicit cast the other way), or change the parameter type if the value may really be null.

choices: Annotate `initialize()` with `@Initializer`
Annotate `mService` with `@MonotonicNonNull`
Annotate the constructor with `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")`
Split setup into several `@Initializer` setters, one per field
explain: For two-phase init, mark the second-phase method `@Initializer`. NullAway doesn't verify it's called, so prefer one `initialize()` over several setters (`onCreate()` is implicitly `@Initializer`).

prompt: You need to silence a NullAway false positive inside one method of a migrated `@NullMarked` class, without weakening checks for its callers. Which annotation do you use?
choices: `@NullUnmarked`
`@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")`
`@Nullable` on the method's return type
Either one; they behave identically
explain: Both suppress warnings in the body, but `@NullUnmarked` makes the signature's nullability unknown to callers. Prefer `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")`; reserve `@NullUnmarked` for code not yet migrated.

choices: `isNull` must be `final` for NullAway to trust it
NullAway needs `assumeNonNull(thing)` after any boolean check
NullAway can't track nullness through booleans; check `thing != null` directly
The warning is a false positive here; add `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")` to the method
explain: NullAway can't follow nullness through intermediate boolean variables (NullAway#98). Put the null check directly in the `if` condition.

prompt: A `@NullMarked` Java class has both `@CalledByNative` methods and Java-to-native calls. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both directions are fully checked by NullAway at compile time
Neither direction is checked, so nullability annotations on native methods are pointless
`@CalledByNative` methods are checked; Java-to-native calls are not
`@CalledByNative` methods aren't null-checked; Java-to-native calls are, via asserts
explain: Nullness isn't checked for `@CalledByNative` methods, but Java-to-native calls are checked via `assert` when `@NullMarked` is present, so annotate native-bound parameters correctly.

prompt: Java code will be mirrored and built outside Chromium. How should nullability annotations be set up?
choices: Use JSpecify (`org_jspecify_jspecify_java`) with `chromium_code = false` and `enable_errorprone = true`
Use `org.chromium.build.annotations` as usual; mirrored builds can simply vendor the `build_java` target
Use AndroidX `@Nullable` from `androidx.annotation`, which both builds already depend on
Omit annotations in mirrored code and set `enable_errorprone = false` in its GN target
explain: For mirrored code, use JSpecify annotations instead of Chromium's copies, add the jspecify dep, set `chromium_code = false` to avoid the `build_java` dep, and keep `enable_errorprone = true`.

prompt: A PR adds `BraveToggleView extends FrameLayout`, a hand-drawn on/off switch for a settings screen. How should the reviewer flag it?
choices: As a blocker: custom reimplementations of Material components aren't allowed in settings
As a `nit:` asking why `MaterialSwitch` or a Brave subclass of it wasn't used
Not at all; custom views give more control over theming
Ask the author to subclass `SwitchCompat` instead
explain: Prefer Material components, which bring motion, accessibility, and theming. Flag custom reimplementations as `nit:` only, never as a blocker, and never flag Brave subclasses of Material components.

prompt: You're adding a new standalone `MyFeatureController.java` (no upstream subclassing) in brave-core. Where should it go?
choices: In `android/java/org/chromium/chrome/browser/my_feature/`, appended to `brave_java_sources`
In `chrome/browser/android/` since that's the shared Android home
In `browser/my_feature/android/` as its own `android_library` in `brave_chrome_java_deps`
In both a feature module and `brave_java_sources`, for compatibility
explain: New feature-specific Java goes in the feature's Android directory (`browser/<feature>/android/`), not the legacy tree. Consumers depend on the feature target; don't also list the files in `brave_java_sources`.
